lead: Axial load stretches or shortens a bar. The extension δ depends on load P, length L, area A and modulus E: δ = P L/(A E). This one relation lets you size a tie rod, check a sag rod in a roof, or predict how much a bolt tightens. A stepped bar adds the extensions of its segments. A compound bar, with two materials bonded side by side, forces both materials to share the same strain and splits the load by stiffness. This chapter builds those two ideas.
prereq: You need: normal stress, Hooke's law and elastic constants.

sections.h3: One uniform bar under axial load

blocks.text: Take a straight bar of length L and constant cross-section A. An axial force P acts along its axis. The bar extends by δ. Strain is ε = δ/L, the fractional change in length. Normal stress is σ = P/A.

items: Hooke's law: σ = E ε, where E is Young's modulus.
Substitute σ and ε: P/A = E δ/L.
Multiply both sides by L and divide by E: δ = P L/(A E).
Check units: N × m /(m² × N/m²) = m.

blocks.where: P is axial force in N; L is original length in m; A is cross-sectional area in m²; E is Young's modulus in N/m² (Pa); δ is extension in m. Positive δ is extension, negative is shortening.

blocks.text: The product A E is axial stiffness in N. A stiffer bar extends less. Use consistent units: 300 mm² = 300 × 10⁻⁶ m². The formula holds while stress is below the proportional limit and the section is uniform.

sections.h3: Stepped bars, varying sections and self weight

blocks.text: A bar made of segments in series carries the same axial force P in every segment. Segment i has length L_i, area A_i and modulus E_i. Its extension is δ_i = P L_i/(A_i E_i). The total extension is the sum of segment extensions. A bolt with a reduced shank and a stepped tie rod are common examples.

blocks.where: i numbers the segments; L_i is length of segment i in m; A_i is its area in m²; E_i is its modulus in N/m²; P is the common axial force in N.

blocks.text: If area changes continuously, replace the sum by an integral. Let x run along the axis from 0 to L, and let A(x) be the area at x. For constant P and E, δ = ∫₀ᴸ P dx/(A(x) E). A tapered round bar needs A(x) = π r(x)² inside the integral.

Self weight: a uniform vertical bar of length L, area A and density ρ hangs from its top. Its total weight is W = ρ g A L, where g is acceleration due to gravity. Some syllabi include the extension δ = ρ g L²/(2E) = W L/(2 A E). The factor 2 appears because the internal force falls from W at the top to zero at the bottom.

Two materials bonded along their length form a compound bar in parallel. Both parts have the same extension δ and the same length L, so both have the same strain ε = δ/L. The load splits: P = P1 + P2. Each material obeys its own Hooke's law: σ1 = E1 ε and σ2 = E2 ε. The forces are P1 = σ1 A1 and P2 = σ2 A2.

blocks.where: P is total axial load in N; A1 and A2 are areas in m²; E1 and E2 are moduli in N/m²; ε is the common strain. Then σ1 = E1 ε and σ2 = E2 ε.

blocks.text: The term A E is axial stiffness. The stiffer material takes a larger share of load, not a larger strain. For more than two materials, add every A_i E_i in the denominator. A steel rod bonded inside an aluminium tube is a standard example. The bond must transfer shear; if it slips, equal strain fails. For several axial loads in the linear elastic range, superposition applies: add the extensions from each load separately. Do not add strains of materials that are in parallel.

examples.question: A steel bar has two parts in series. Part 1 has length 0.4 m and area 300 mm². Part 2 has length 0.6 m and area 200 mm². E = 200 GPa and the axial load is 40 kN. Find the total elongation.
steps: Both parts are in series, so add extensions: δ = δ1 + δ2 = 0.2667 + 0.6000 = 0.8667 mm.

traps: Using the total load for every segment is correct, but using the total length or one area for all segments is wrong: each segment has its own L_i and A_i.
In a compound bar in parallel, adding strains is wrong. Both materials share the same strain; the loads add.
Mixing mm² and m² in δ = P L/(A E) gives answers off by 10⁶. Convert area to m² first.
Putting E in GPa directly into the formula gives a result in the wrong units. Use N/m²: 200 GPa = 200 × 10⁹ N/m².
In a hanging bar under self weight, using δ = W L/(A E) misses the factor 1/2; the axial force varies along the length.

quiz.q: Write the axial extension formula for a uniform bar and state the meaning of each symbol.
quiz.a: δ = P L/(A E). P is axial force in N, L is original length in m, A is area in m², E is Young's modulus in N/m², δ is extension in m.

quiz.q: Why does a stepped bar add the extensions of its segments instead of using one average area?
quiz.a: Each segment carries the same axial force P but has its own L, A and E. Its extension is P L_i/(A_i E_i). The total change in length is the sum of the segment changes, because the segments are in series.

quiz.q: A steel rod of area 200 mm², E = 200 GPa, is bonded inside an aluminium tube of area 300 mm², E = 70 GPa. The compound bar carries 100 kN. Find the stress in each material.
A uniform vertical bar hangs under its own weight. Where is the axial stress largest, and what is the extension formula?
quiz.a: Stress is largest at the top, where the internal force equals the whole weight W. It is zero at the free bottom. The extension is δ = ρgL²/(2E) = W L/(2AE). The factor 1/2 comes from the linearly varying force.

quiz.q: Two segments in series: L1 = 0.5 m, A1 = 400 mm²; L2 = 0.5 m, A2 = 200 mm². E = 200 GPa, P = 20 kN. Find total extension.
In a compound bar in parallel, why does the stiffer material carry more load?
quiz.a: Both materials have the same strain ε. Stress is σ = Eε, so a larger E gives larger stress. Load share is σA, so the material with larger A E carries more load.

quiz.q: A steel core and an aluminium sleeve have equal areas and are bonded along their length. Steel E is three times aluminium E. Compare their stresses and loads under axial load.
quiz.a: They share the same strain ε. σsteel = Esteel ε and σaluminium = Ealuminium ε, so σsteel/σaluminium = 3. With equal areas, Psteel/Paluminium = 3. The steel carries three times the load of the aluminium.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite element codes build every truss and frame from axial bar elements that use exactly δ = P L/(A E) and an assembly of parallel stiffnesses. Composite insulators, prestressed concrete tendons and bonded repair patches all rely on equal-strain load sharing. Search next for “axial bar finite element stiffness matrix”, “composite bar compatibility” and “self weight of a hanging bar”.
